MESSAGE:
Hi. I'm off to Lisbon next week for a three-day work trip, my first time in Portugal, and I want to travel carry-on only this time, after the airline lost my case in the spring.

Could you suggest three things to do in Lisbon on a free evening? And how do I say "thank you" in Portuguese? Is it different depending on who's saying it? And is tipping expected in restaurants there, or is that more of an American thing?

My wheeled bag measures 56 × 36 × 23 cm including the wheels and handle, and packed it weighs 9 kg. Will it meet the carry-on limit?

Also, recommend a packing approach: rolling or folding for work shirts? I need a short out-of-office message that's professional but not stiff, since most of my contacts are clients rather than colleagues. And what's a good colour for a luggage tag so it's easy to spot? I'm flying back on the Friday evening, straight after a full day of meetings, so anything that makes the return journey less stressful is welcome.

Thanks a lot.

RESPONSE:
# Lisbon Trip Notes

## Three things to do on a free evening

1. **Watch the sunset from a miradouro (viewpoint).** Try Miradouro da Senhora do Monte, which has the widest view, or Miradouro de Santa Catarina, which is livelier and has a kiosk bar. In mid-November the sun sets around 17:20, so go straight after work.
2. **Hear fado in Alfama or Mouraria.** This is Lisbon's traditional music, and it's best in a small *tasca* rather than a big dinner-show venue. Tasca do Chico (Bairro Alto) and Mesa de Frades (Alfama) are well-known options. Book ahead or arrive early, and stay quiet during songs; locals take that seriously.
3. **Have dinner and drinks in Bairro Alto or Príncipe Real.** Bairro Alto has narrow streets packed with small bars, and Príncipe Real is calmer and more upscale. For something easy, Time Out Market in Cais do Sodré lets you sample lots of Portuguese dishes in one place. Try a *pastel de nata* and a glass of *ginjinha* (cherry liqueur) at some point.

## Saying "thank you"

It depends on **who is speaking**, not who you're thanking:
- **Obrigado** (oh-bree-GAH-doo) if you're a man
- **Obrigada** (oh-bree-GAH-dah) if you're a woman

It literally means "obliged," so it agrees with the speaker. **Muito obrigado/a** means "thank you very much."

## Tipping

Tipping isn't expected the way it is in the US, and staff don't depend on it.
- **Cafés and casual places:** leaving small change or rounding up is normal.
- **Sit-down restaurants:** about 5–10% for good service is appreciated but optional.
- Check the bill first. If you see a "serviço" charge, you don't need to add more.
- **Taxis:** rounding up is enough.

## Will your bag meet the carry-on limit?

Possibly not. You didn't mention your airline, and limits vary, but your bag is borderline on several common rules:

| | Your bag | Common limits |
|---|---|---|
| Height | **56 cm** | 55 cm (most European airlines) |
| Width | 36 cm | 35–40 cm |
| Depth | 23 cm | 20–25 cm (TAP Air Portugal: 20 cm) |
| Weight | **9 kg** | Often 7–8 kg in economy; some airlines allow 10 kg or more, or have no limit |

At 56 cm you're 1 cm over the most common height limit. Strict gate checks, especially on budget carriers, may make you check it, which is what you're trying to avoid.

**What to do:**
- Check your airline's limits for your **specific fare type**, since basic fares often allow only a small under-seat bag.
- Get the weight down to 8 kg or less. Wear your heaviest shoes and jacket on the plane, and move your laptop and chargers into a personal-item bag if one is allowed.
- If the bag bulges, pack it less full so the depth stays within the limit.

Tell me the airline and fare and I'll give you a clearer answer.

## Rolling or folding work shirts?

**Fold them.** Rolling suits T-shirts, knitwear and casual clothes, but it leaves small creases in crisp cotton shirts.
- Button the shirts, fold them around a flat core (a folder works), and stack them collar to tail, alternating direction.
- Slip each one into a dry-cleaning bag or tissue paper to cut down creasing.
- Wear one shirt on the plane.
- Hotels nearly always have an iron. Hanging a shirt in a steamy bathroom also helps.
- Roll everything else around the shirt stack to fill gaps and save space.

## Out-of-office message

> Hello,
>
> Thank you for your email. I'm travelling for work from [date] to [date] and will have limited access to email during that time. I'll reply as soon as I can after I'm back on [date].
>
> If your request is urgent, please contact [name] at [email/phone], who will be happy to help.
>
> Best regards,
> [Your name]

It sounds warm without being casual. You could replace "who will be happy to help" with "who can help in the meantime" if you prefer.

## Luggage tag colour

Pick something **bright and unusual**: neon orange, lime green or hot pink stand out against all the black and navy bags. A tag paired with a bright strap or ribbon is even easier to spot. Even with carry-on only, this helps if your bag gets checked at the gate or ends up in a crowded overhead bin.

Use your name, phone number and email on the tag, but **not your home address**.

## Making the Friday return easier

- **Pack Thursday night** so only your toiletries and Friday clothes are left out.
- **Check out in the morning** and leave your bag at the hotel, or bring it to your meetings if that works better.
- **Check in online** and download your boarding pass the day before.
- **Leave plenty of time.** Lisbon airport is close to the city (about 20–30 minutes by taxi or Uber, or the metro red line), but it's busy and security queues can be long. Aim to arrive about 2 hours before departure.
- **Keep liquids in a ready-to-remove bag** at the top of your luggage.
- **Wear something comfortable on Friday**, or bring a change for the flight.
- **Buy snacks or dinner after security** so you aren't rushing to eat beforehand.

Have a great trip, and *boa viagem*!
